extracted.intended_audience: students, educators, and professional mathematicians interested in mathematical methodology, numerical analysis, and the nature of mathematical exposition
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative criteria for mathematical work (especially numerical analysis, theorem formulation, and exposition). Covers what makes algorithms, proofs, and presentations 'good' or comprehensible, and tradeoffs between algorithmic concreteness and abstract generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of error bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Error bounds may be deterministic or statistical; a priori or a posteriori; only approximate or asymptotic; and may even be bounds that the computer itself has computed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When performing error analysis, state which kind(s) of bounds are being produced, and whether they are computable before the main computation (a priori) or require the computation to be carried out (a posteriori). Note whether bounds are probabilistic or deterministic and whether they are exact, approximate, or asymptotic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing and handling blunders
rubrics_metrics.description: Blunders should not be lightly dismissed — they occur with sufficient frequency that the practicing numerical analyst must learn how to recognize them and how to deal with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In numerical work include procedures for detecting catastrophic mistakes (implementation or model blunders) and protocols for diagnosing and correcting them rather than assuming numerical output is automatically reliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of a good numerical answer (residual vs error)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different possible criteria: an answer x̂ may be 'good' if |x* − x̂| is small (closeness to exact solution) or if f(x̂) is approximately zero (small residual), and if f itself can only be computed approximately this affects which criterion is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state which criterion you adopt when judging numerical results; consider availability/accuracy of f, stability of the problem, and whether residual smallness implies solution closeness in the given context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence theory and rate of convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Can we obtain answers of increasing accuracy by a fixed type of algorithm? Numerical analysis studies convergence including the rate of convergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing or analyzing an algorithm, provide convergence proofs or empirical evidence of convergence and quantify the convergence rate (e.g., linear, quadratic), since this determines practical usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components of a complete numerical analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete numerical analysis of any problem would consist of: 1) The formation of algorithms. 2) Error analysis, including truncation and roundoff error. 3) The study of convergence including the rate of convergence. 4) Comparison of algorithms to judge relative utility in different situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to address all four components when presenting numerical work: design the algorithm, analyze/estimate errors, prove or empirically establish convergence and its rate, and compare with alternatives on representative problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic attitude vs dialectical (theoretical) attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The pure algorithmic spirit would be content with inventing algorithms and trying them out in typical problems (practical experience); the dialectical viewpoint demands careful error analysis, convergence proofs, and rate estimates (theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about which stance you are taking: practical algorithm-designers may justify methods by computational experience, while theoreticians require rigorous proofs and bounds. Both attitudes are legitimate but have different standards of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical testing on typical problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The algorithmic attitude tests algorithms 'in typical problems to see how they work'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include representative computational experiments and benchmarks to demonstrate practical performance and robustness across typical problem instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoff between algorithmic concreteness and abstract structural formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A formulation emphasizing structure (abstraction) may give less information about concrete algorithms for computation, while an arithmetic/algorithmic formulation gives explicit methods; generality can 'give us less and more' than previous formulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When generalizing, explicitly note what computational procedures are lost or obscured and, if relevant, supply concrete algorithms or constructions to retain computational usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for examples and operational intuition in abstract presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: A paucity of examples in a highly abstract formulation makes the statement remote and incomprehensible to many readers; illumination often requires examples and 'mulling and pondering'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accompany abstract/general theorems with concrete examples and demonstrations showing how abstract concepts operate in familiar settings to aid comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical definitions/axioms for groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws for mathematical groups: (1) closure (combination of two elements is in G), (2) associativity, (3) identity element, (4) inverses for every element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defining algebraic structures, present the axioms clearly and give motivating examples and non-examples so readers can grasp the intended concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard group-theoretic notions: order, subgroup, normal subgroup, simple group, cyclic group
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: 'order' is number of elements; subgroup is subset that is itself a group; normal subgroup H satisfies gHg^{-1} ⊆ H; simple groups have no nontrivial normal subgroups; cyclic groups have elements generating the whole group by successive powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working in finite group theory, explicitly state and use these notions; provide examples and use the notions to decompose and analyze group structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lagrange's theorem (subgroup order divides group order)
rubrics_metrics.description: By Lagrange one knows that the order of a subgroup always divides the order of the group itself; consequence: groups of prime order have no nontrivial subgroups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Lagrange's theorem as a basic structural tool in reasoning about finite groups and in eliminating impossible subgroup sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central research goal: classification of finite simple groups
rubrics_metrics.description: The main goal of finite group theory is to give a complete classification of all the 'simple groups'—analogous to the role of primes in number theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame major projects or expository sections in terms of their contribution toward this classification goal, and note methodological implications (e.g., complex, long proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability and implications of very long, detailed proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory of simple finite groups is notable for 'unprecedented length and detail of its proofs'; such proofs are a methodological feature of certain fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting or evaluating work with long proofs, discuss verification strategies, modular organization, and how the length affects accessibility and acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of computation and experience to inform theoretical judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems like the twin primes 'exhibit the importance of experience and calculation in arriving at theoretical judgments'; computational evidence can guide conjecture and theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report computational experiments and heuristic observations clearly, distinguishing them from proofs, and use them to motivate conjectures or to test plausibility of theoretical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/formal clarity: specify uniqueness/existence issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical treatments (e.g., Sun Tzu, Fibonacci) sometimes omit questions of uniqueness; modern formulations should explicitly address existence and uniqueness of solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In problem statements and theorems, explicitly state existence and uniqueness results and provide conditions under which they hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give operational meaning to new concepts introduced by internal mathematical necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: When internal necessities of mathematics create new objects (e.g., complex numbers arising in Cardano's formula), provide interpretations (geometric, algebraic) that legitimize and operationalize them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming or using novel constructs, supply definitions, examples, and interpretations (e.g., complex numbers as plane points) that make them usable and meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of unification (connecting disparate ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unification (establishment of relations between seemingly diverse objects) is a great motivating force and source of aesthetic satisfaction in mathematics (e.g., Euler's formula connecting exponentials and trigonometry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, highlight unifying perspectives that show how different areas connect, and use such unification to motivate deeper study or applications.
